title: URI Template
summary: A URI Template is a compact string describing a range of URIs through variable expansion. This RFC defines the syntax, the process for expanding a template into a URI reference, and guidelines for using templates on the Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: A URI template is a short string with gaps in it that stands for a whole family of web addresses. A program fills the gaps with values and gets back a proper address, with the right escaping applied each time. The RFC defines the syntax and the filling rules so that different programs produce the same address from the same template.

questions: how to expand a uri template
what do the uri template operators mean
what is the explode modifier in uri templates
how are uri template values escaped
subtitle: A compact string with blanks in it that describes a whole family of URIs, and exactly how to fill the blanks in.

tldr.problem: Services often publish many similar URIs, such as one per user or one per search, and had no single agreed way to describe the pattern so that software could build the right URI from some values.
tldr.mechanism: A URI Template embeds expressions in braces, such as {term} or {?q,lang}. A template processor replaces each expression with the encoded values of its variables, following rules set by an optional operator and by Level 4 value modifiers.
tldr.outcome: Templates and the expansion rules are defined once, in four levels of increasing power, so different applications can share them. RFC 6570 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 6570 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012. The metadata for this unit records no later RFC that obsoletes or updating it. The document defines the template syntax and the expansion process, and states that earlier mechanisms of a similar kind, in WSDL, WADL and OpenSearch, are extended by it rather than replaced.

sections.title: What a URI Template Is
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Identifier is often used to identify a specific resource within a common space of similar resources, informally a URI space. Personal web spaces are often delegated using a common pattern, such as http://example.com/~fred/, a set of dictionary entries might be grouped in a hierarchy by the first letter of the term, as in http://example.com/dictionary/c/cat, and a service interface might be invoked with various user input in a common pattern, as in http://example.com/search?q=cat&lang=en.

A URI Template is a compact sequence of characters for describing a range of Uniform Resource Identifiers through variable expansion. It provides a mechanism for abstracting a space of resource identifiers so that the variable parts can be easily identified and described. Templates have many uses, including the discovery of available services, configuring resource mappings, defining computed links, specifying interfaces and other forms of programmatic interaction with resources. The examples above could be described by the templates http://example.com/~{username}/, http://example.com/dictionary/{term:1}/{term} and http://example.com/search{?q,lang}.

The document defines an expression as the text between braces, including the braces, and an expansion as the string result obtained from a template expression after processing it according to its expression type, list of variable names and value modifiers. A template processor is a program or library that, given a URI Template and a set of variables with values, transforms the template string into a URI reference by parsing the template for expressions and substituting each one with its corresponding expansion.

A template gives both a structural description of a URI space and, when variable values are provided, machine-readable instructions on how to construct a URI for those values. The expansions are based on the URI generic syntax, so an implementation can process any template without knowing the scheme-specific requirements of every possible resulting URI.
sections.plainLanguage: Many services hand out addresses that differ only in one or two places, such as a username or a search word. A template writes that pattern down once, so that a program can build the right address without the pattern being written out again for every case.

sections.title: Four Levels of Power
sections.content:
URI Templates are similar to a macro language with a fixed set of macro definitions: the expression type determines the expansion process. The default expression type is simple string expansion, where a single named variable is replaced by its value as a string after pct-encoding any characters not in the set of unreserved URI characters. Since most template processors implemented before this specification had only implemented the default expression type, these are called Level 1 templates.

Level 2 templates add the plus operator, for expansion of values that are allowed to include reserved URI characters, and the crosshatch operator for expansion of fragment identifiers. With the variable path set to /foo/bar, the template {+path}/here expands to /foo/bar/here, and {+hello} expands to Hello%20World!.

Level 3 templates allow multiple variables per expression, each separated by a comma, and add more complex operators for dot-prefixed labels, slash-prefixed path segments, semicolon-prefixed path parameters, and the form-style construction of a query syntax consisting of name=value pairs separated by an ampersand character. With the variables x and y set to 1024 and 768, {?x,y} expands to ?x=1024&y=768.

Level 4 templates add value modifiers as an optional suffix to each variable name. A prefix modifier indicates that only a limited number of characters from the beginning of the value are used by the expansion, and an explode modifier indicates that the variable is to be treated as a composite value, consisting of either a list of names or an associative array of name and value pairs, expanded as if each member were a separate variable. With var set to value, {var:3} expands to val.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules come in four sizes. The simplest just puts a value in the middle of a string. The next ones add ways to build a path segment, a query string or a fragment. The largest adds ways to cut a value short and to expand a list of values.

sections.title: The Grammar
sections.content:
A URI Template is a string of printable Unicode characters that contains zero or more embedded variable expressions, each delimited by a matching pair of braces. The syntax is defined with the ABNF for Level 4, and a processor limited to lower-level templates MAY exclude the rules applicable only to higher levels, although it is RECOMMENDED that all parsers implement the full syntax so that unsupported levels can be identified as such to the end user.

The characters outside expressions are literals. A literal character is copied literally to the URI reference if it is allowed in a URI, and otherwise copied as the sequence of pct-encoded triplets corresponding to that character's encoding in UTF-8.

Each expression contains an optional operator, which defines the expression type and its expansion process, followed by a comma-separated list of variable specifiers, made up of variable names and optional value modifiers. If no operator is provided, the expression defaults to simple variable expansion of unreserved values. The operator characters have been chosen to reflect each of their roles as reserved characters in the URI generic syntax. The plus sign + stands for reserved character strings, the crosshatch operator for fragment identifiers prefixed by a crosshatch, the dot . for name labels or extensions, the slash / for path segments, the semicolon ; for path parameter names or name=value pairs, the question mark ? for a query component of name=value pairs separated by an ampersand, and the ampersand & for the continuation of query-style pairs within a literal query component. The characters equals, comma, exclamation, at sign and pipe are reserved for future extensions. The expression syntax specifically excludes the dollar and parenthesis characters so that they remain available for use outside the scope of this specification.

Variable names serve multiple purposes: documentation for what kinds of values are expected, identifiers for associating values within a template processor, and the literal string to use for the name in name=value expansions. Variable names are case-sensitive because the name might be expanded within a case-sensitive URI component. An expression MAY reference variables that are unknown to the template processor or whose value is set to a special undefined value, such as undef or null. A variable value that is a string of length zero is not considered undefined; it has the defined value of an empty string. A list variable is considered undefined if the list has no members, and an associative array is undefined if it has no members or if all member names are associated with undefined values.
sections.plainLanguage: A template is plain text with expressions in braces. Each expression starts with an optional punctuation mark that says what kind of address part is being built, then a list of variable names, each with an optional modifier.

sections.title: How Expansion Works
sections.content:
Expansion scans the template from beginning to end, copying literal characters and replacing each expression with the result of applying the expression's operator to the value of each variable named in the expression. Each variable's value MUST be formed before template expansion. If a template processor encounters a character sequence outside an expression that does not match the grammar, processing SHOULD cease, the result SHOULD contain the expanded part followed by the remainder unexpanded, and the location and type of error SHOULD be indicated to the invoking application. If an error is encountered inside an expression, such as an unrecognized operator or value modifier, the unprocessed parts SHOULD be copied to the result unexpanded and processing of the remainder SHOULD continue. If an error occurs, the result returned might not be a valid URI reference; it will be an incompletely expanded template string intended for diagnostic use.

An undefined variable has no value and is ignored. If all the variables in an expression are undefined, the expansion is the empty string. The allowed characters depend on the expression type: reserved and fragment expansions allow the union of unreserved, reserved and pct-encoded characters to pass through without pct-encoding, while all other expression types allow only unreserved characters. The percent character is only allowed as part of a pct-encoded triplet and only for reserved or fragment expansion; in all other cases it MUST be pct-encoded as %25.

A simple string value is expanded by appending the encoded value to the result. A prefix modifier limits the expansion to the first max-length characters of the decoded value, counting each Unicode code point as one character to avoid splitting a multi-octet character. A variable that is an associative array expands as a comma-separated concatenation of each defined name and value pair, or, with an explode modifier, as each pair written as name=value, with the separator chosen by the expression type: a comma by default and for the reserved and fragment types, a dot for label expansion, a slash for path segments, a semicolon for path-style parameters, and an ampersand for form-style queries. A list value expands as a comma-separated concatenation of its defined members, or, with an explode modifier, as separate variables separated by the type's separator, unless the type expands named parameters, in which case the list is treated as an array whose members are all paired with the list's variable name.
sections.plainLanguage: Expansion is a single pass over the template. Each expression is replaced by the values of its variables, escaped according to the rules of its operator. Values that were never set are simply left out.

sections.title: The Operators in Action
sections.content:
Simple string expansion is the default when no operator is given, and it allows only unreserved characters through. With var set to value and hello set to Hello World!, the template {var} expands to value and {hello} expands to Hello%20World%21. A value of 50% becomes 50%25. With two variables, {x,hello,y} expands to 1024,Hello%20World%21,768, the values joined by commas.

Reserved expansion, marked with the plus operator, is identical to simple string expansion except that the substituted values may also contain pct-encoded triplets and characters in the reserved set. A value of http://example.com/home/ becomes http://example.com/home/index in {+base}index, while in {base}index the same value becomes http%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Fhome%2Findex.

Fragment expansion, marked with the crosshatch, is identical to reserved expansion except that a crosshatch character is appended first to the result string if any of the variables are defined. So {#var} expands to #value, while foo{#empty} expands to foo# and foo{#undef} expands to foo.

The remaining operators follow the same pattern. Label expansion with a dot gives X{.var} as X.value. Path segment expansion with a slash gives {/var} as /value. Path-style parameter expansion with a semicolon gives {;x,y} as ;x=1024;y=768. Form-style query expansion with a question mark gives {?x,y} as ?x=1024&y=768, and continuation with an ampersand gives ?fixed=yes{&x} as ?fixed=yes&x=1024. In the path-style form an empty value drops the equals sign, so {;x,y,empty} expands to ;x=1024;y=768;empty, while the form-style form keeps it, giving ?x=1024&y=768&empty=.
sections.plainLanguage: Each punctuation mark picks a different shape for the filled-in result. A dot makes a label, a slash makes a path segment, a question mark makes a query string, and the crosshatch starts the fragment part of the address.

sections.title: Characters and Normalization
sections.content:
The specification defines its terminal values as code points within the Unicode coded character set. In spite of the syntax and template expansion process being defined in terms of Unicode code points, templates occur in practice as a sequence of characters in whatever form or encoding suits the context, whether octets embedded in a network protocol element or glyphs painted on the side of a bus. No particular character encoding scheme is mandated for mapping between template characters and the octets used to store or transmit them; when a template appears in a protocol element, the encoding scheme is defined by that protocol, and without such a definition the template is assumed to be in the same encoding scheme as the surrounding text. It is only during template expansion that the characters of a template are REQUIRED to be processed as a sequence of Unicode code points.

The Unicode Standard defines equivalences between sequences of characters, and its Annex 15 defines various normalization forms for these equivalences. In theory all URI processing implementations, including template processors, should use the same normalization form, but in practice they do not. If a value has been provided by the same server as the resource, the string can be assumed to be in the form that server expects. If a value is provided by a user, such as through a data-entry dialog, the string SHOULD be normalized as Normalization Form C, canonical decomposition followed by canonical composition, before being used in expansions.

Likewise, when non-ASCII data that represents readable strings is pct-encoded for use in a URI reference, a template processor MUST first encode the string as UTF-8 and then pct-encode any octets that are not allowed in a URI reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The same visible character can be stored in more than one way. Before a value goes into an address, the processor encodes it as UTF-8 and then escapes the bytes that are not allowed, so the result is always the same for the same text.

sections.title: What Templates Are Not
sections.content:
Since a URI Template describes a superset of the identifiers, there is no implication that every possible expansion for each delimited variable expression corresponds to a URI of an existing resource. The expectation is that an application constructing URIs according to the template will be provided with an appropriate set of values for the variables being substituted, or at least a means of validating user data entry for those values.

URI Templates are not URIs: they do not identify an abstract or physical resource, they are not parsed as URIs, and they should not be used in places where a URI would be expected unless the template expressions will be expanded by a template processor prior to use. Distinct field, element or attribute names should be used to differentiate protocol elements that carry a URI Template from those that expect a URI reference.

Some templates can be used in reverse for variable matching, comparing the template to a fully formed URI in order to extract the variable parts and assign them to the named variables. Variable matching only works well if the template expressions are delimited by the beginning or end of the URI or by characters that cannot be part of the expansion, such as reserved characters surrounding a simple string expression. In general, regular expression languages are better suited for variable matching.
sections.plainLanguage: A template is a pattern, not an address. Filling it in can produce an address that does not exist, so the program filling it in has to supply sensible values. The RFC also says matching an address back to a template is a poor fit for it, and that regular expressions do that job better.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A URI Template does not contain active or executable content. However, it might be possible to craft unanticipated URIs if an attacker is given control over the template or over the variable values within an expression that allows reserved characters in the expansion. In either case, the security considerations are largely determined by who provides the template, who provides the values to use for variables within the template, in what execution context the expansion occurs, client or server, and where the resulting URIs are used.

The specification does not limit where URI Templates might be used; current implementations exist within server-side development frameworks and within client-side JavaScript for computed links or forms. Within frameworks, templates usually act as guides for where data might occur within later request-time URIs in client requests, so the security concerns are not in the templates themselves but rather in how the server extracts and processes user-provided data within a normal web request.

Within client-side implementations, a URI Template has many of the same properties as HTML forms, except limited to URI characters and possibly included in HTTP header field values instead of just message body content. Care ought to be taken to ensure that potentially dangerous URI reference strings, such as those beginning with javascript:, do not appear in the expansion unless both the template and the values are provided by a trusted source. Other security considerations are the same as those for URIs, as described in Section 7 of RFC 3986.
sections.plainLanguage: The template itself is harmless text. The risk comes from who chooses the values: a value that smuggles in a dangerous scheme, such as javascript:, can end up in the address that the browser follows. That is why the RFC says to trust the values only when the template and the values come from a trusted source.

viz.caption: THE TEMPLATE GRAMMAR FROM RFC 6570 SECTION 2

data.title: URI-Template grammar
data.code:
URI-Template  = *( literals / expression )

expression    =  "{" [ operator ] variable-list "}"
operator      =  op-level2 / op-level3 / op-reserve
op-level2     =  "+" / "#"
op-level3     =  "." / "/" / ";" / "?" / "&"
op-reserve    =  "=" / "," / "!" / "@" / "|"

variable-list =  varspec *( "," varspec )
varspec       =  varname [ modifier-level4 ]
varname       =  varchar *( ["."] varchar )
varchar       =  ALPHA / DIGIT / "_" / pct-encoded

modifier-level4 =  prefix / explode
prefix        =  ":" max-length
max-length    =  %x31-39 0*3DIGIT   ; positive integer < 10000

viz.caption: THE OPERATORS AND WHAT THEY BUILD

items.label: Simple string
items.desc: The default: the value replaces the expression, escaped to unreserved characters.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Reserved characters in the value are left as they are.

items.label: Fragment
items.desc: Like the reserved form, but a crosshatch is added first.

items.label: Label
items.desc: Builds a dotted label, as in X.value.

items.label: Path segment
items.desc: Builds a path segment, as in /value.

items.label: Form-style query
items.desc: Builds a query string, as in ?x=1024&y=768.

items.label: Query continuation
items.desc: Adds more pairs to a query that is already there.

cells: Simple string expansion, one variable per expression
The + and # operators, still one variable per expression
Several variables per expression, and the . / ; ? & operators
Value modifiers: a prefix and an explode modifier
